newsitem.title: UK: Copper's surges 5 pct in one volatile day.
newsitem.headline: Copper's surges 5 pct in one volatile day.

text.p: The world price of copper shot up by five per cent on Friday to the highest in 2-1/2 months in a stunning rally based on concern about low stocks.
Volatility gripped trading in the flagship industrial metal.
"I'm not prepared to call the next $50 move. It could happen in the wink of an eye," one trader said.
Copper began the day by sagging as low as $2,010 per tonne on fears that stocks might be bigger than they seem.

Then the market discounted those concerns and soared to reach $2,152 on fresh data that showed stock volumes held in warehouses supervised by the London Metal Exchange (LME) were at the lowest since 1990.
The latest draw on these LME stocks reduced them by 8,000 tonnes to 101,175 or less than a week's world demand.
"The market reacted to that, because it had been pushed lower on some talk of a stock increase. That has forced the shorts to cover," a trader said.

Earlier this week a UK-based statistical body, the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), alarmed the market by suggesting that nearly 600,000 tonnes of copper not previously reported may have built up in Netherlands bonded warehouses between 1991 and 1995.

Analyst Martin Squires of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co said, "The issue has been clouded by the reports of statistical errors in counting the level of stock movement in and out of Rotterdam over the past few years." Elsewhere in commodity markets, gold's strong performance this week turned sour on Friday after heavy selling linked to speculators and mining firms erased recent gains and took it down to a London close at $379.75 an ounce. Analysts expected that gold would now hold above the $377-$379 area.
Crude oil prices lost the high gained on Thursday when an early cold snap brought oil companies rushing to replenish low heating fuel stocks ahead of demand in the northern hemisphere.
The world benchmark Brent crude oil futures stood at around $23.50 per barrel late in the London afternoon, down about 25 cents overnight but well above an early-November low of $22.11.
Wheat prices in Chicago held their three-week highs from earlier in the week at around $4.00 per bushel which was achieved on bullish export prospects.
Despite the December sugar futures contract expiring in London, sugar and the other soft commodites were featureless.
One leading commission house was reported to be selling any December sugar positions in the few hours remaining before expiry, and some light trade buying of the position was also seen.
